scope: Selected primary/theory/institutional physics sources; not an exhaustive literature review and not a conference-ranking claim.

sources.title: On the Vibrations of an Elastic Sphere
sources.venue: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, s1-13, 189–212
sources.reading_depth: Publisher bibliographic record; full original paper not read.
sources.claim: Historical origin of the elastic-sphere mode problem; the implemented boundary expression is checked in the accessible 2005 primary paper.
sources.caveat: Publisher issue date is November1881; later literature commonly cites1882. Preserve this bibliographic distinction.

sources.title: Longitudinal versus transverse spheroidal vibrational modes of an elastic sphere
sources.authors: Lucien Saviot and Daniel B. Murray
sources.reading_depth: Full SectionII free-sphere formulation, equations1–3 and l=0 reduction; SectionIII opening and derivative interpretation; abstract and original metadata.
sources.claim: A homogeneous isotropic traction-free sphere has distinct torsional and spheroidal families. Radial l=0 modes use the T11 boundary condition, with size and sound-speed dependence.
sources.caveat: The HTML conversion displays an August2026 date; original version/publication metadata establish2005. Selected l=0 implementation is not full-mode completeness.

sources.title: Vibrational eigenmodes of an isotropic sphere
sources.reading_depth: Full explanatory page and reference list; interactive outputs were not used as the independent numerical implementation.
sources.claim: Useful external mode-family tool and reference; inputs are longitudinal/transverse speeds, diameter, family and indices.
sources.caveat: The page specifically warns about an incorrect spheroidal l=0 frequency expression in a cited textbook. Its disclaimer is use at own risk.

sources.title: Elastic Properties of Metals and Alloys. II. Copper
sources.venue: Journal of Physical and Chemical Reference Data3,897
sources.reading_depth: Introduction, Sections9–10, Table10 (PDFpage28/printed923), Table12 (PDFpage30/printed925), selected density entries in Table9.
sources.claim: Compiled copper elastic properties distinguish polycrystal effective values, single-crystal constants, temperature and processing effects. Table10 averages E123.5GPa and nu0.350 inform illustrative defaults.
sources.caveat: Literature averages and their standard errors are not a certificate of the proposed ball. Independently averaged constants may not obey one exact isotropic identity. Density8960kg/m3 is a rounded illustrative input.

sources.title: On the establishment of a method for characterization of material microstructure through laser-based resonant ultrasound spectroscopy
sources.authors: Stephen J. Reese, Kenneth L. Telschow, Thomas M. Lillo and David H. Hurley
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics, and Frequency Control55(4),770–776
sources.reading_depth: Institutional abstract and metadata; full paper not read.
sources.claim: Laser-based RUS was applied to high-purity polycrystalline copper, comparing measured modes with elastic constants informed by microstructure.
sources.caveat: This demonstrates a relevant approach, not the current project's proposed A/B experiment or its achievable precision.

sources.title: Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy and homogeneity in polycrystals
sources.authors: Gunes Kaplan, T.W. Darling and K.R. McCall
sources.reading_depth: Primary abstract via PubMed and publication metadata; full paper not read.
sources.claim: Pure copper's grain-size distribution can violate the homogeneous effective model assumed when interpreting RUS.
sources.caveat: The source's particular observed grain-size criterion is sample/study-specific and is not adopted as a universal acceptance threshold here. Online publication2008, journal issue2009.

sources.title: Resonance ultrasonic spectroscopy applied to normal and tangential contact modes investigation of a constrained metallic sphere
sources.authors: M. de Billy and F. Cohen Tenoudji
sources.reading_depth: Primary abstract, highlights and bibliographic records; full paper not read.
sources.claim: A compressed steel sphere has contact-conditioned low-frequency motion in addition to internal deformation modes; applied force changes contact spectral peaks.
sources.caveat: Material and loading differ from the proposed copper experiment. The browser's spring example is pedagogical, not a reproduced fit to this experiment.
